# wanderbar

> Takes one GPX track, works out roughly where you are along it, and shows the
> weather for the rest of it as a time-ordered timeline. Notifies only when
> conditions worsen or clear. Installable PWA; all weather logic runs in the
> browser.

wanderbar is free, needs no account, and stores your track, position and
forecasts only in your own browser. The server keeps one push subscription and
one schedule, nothing else.

## What it does

- Parses a recorded GPX track and resamples it to at most 60 waypoints.
- Derives an ETA per waypoint from published pace standards: DIN 33466 and DAV
  for hiking, the SAC scale for mountain terrain, VAM benchmarks for cycling,
  and the SAC/DAV winter rate for hiking on snow. These count moving time only,
  so rest is a separate multiplier the user picks.
- Fetches an hourly forecast per waypoint and evaluates warnings against
  user-set thresholds for rain, hail, wind, snow, heat, blizzard, thunderstorm,
  darkness, fire danger, freezing rain, wind chill and lying snow.
- Diffs each sync against the previous warning set and notifies only on change.
- Relays the official avalanche bulletin for the route where one exists (SLF,
  avalanche.report, Varsom/NVE, Avalanche Canada), and says explicitly when one
  does not.

## Deliberate limits, worth quoting accurately

- It is a best-effort forecast from public models. It can be wrong, late or
  missing, and mountain weather turns faster than any forecast follows. It is one
  input to a person's own judgement, never a reason to set out.
- No routing engine. A sparse route-only GPX is rejected with an explicit
  message, never expanded into a track.
- Fire danger is computed on the device (Canadian Fire Weather Index, Van Wagner
  & Pickett 1985) from 60 days of Open-Meteo history, because no public service
  offers a free point-query FWI. Inputs are sampled at local solar noon, as the
  system is calibrated on noon-LST observations, with rain as the 24 h total
  ending at noon. It is an indication and never a substitute for an official
  fire ban.
- Avalanche danger is never computed, only relayed from an official bulletin.
  It depends on the structure of the snowpack and on weak layers buried weeks
  earlier, which no weather forecast exposes. Where no bulletin covers the
  route, where the season has ended, where the bulletin has expired, or where
  the fetch failed, wanderbar says so in those words and shows no danger level.
  An absent bulletin is never an all-clear, and wanderbar knows neither slope
  angle nor aspect, which is most of what decides whether ground slides. The
  bulletin is a pointer to the issuing service, never a substitute for reading
  it, and never a reason to go.
- Wind chill is computed on the device from the JAG/TI 2001 model published by
  the US NWS and Environment Canada, not read from a "feels like" variable, and
  is left undefined outside that model's stated range rather than extrapolated.
  Frostbite times quoted alongside it are Environment Canada's bands.
- Deep lying snow is warned about, but wanderbar cannot know whether a track has
  already been broken, which is the single biggest factor in how long a winter
  day actually takes. The warning reports the snow; judging the trail-breaking
  is the party's own.
- Available in English (/), German (/de) and French (/fr). It is one screen in
  three languages, with reciprocal hreflang; the bare root negotiates from
  Accept-Language, and a reader's explicit choice is remembered. Avalanche
  bulletins are the exception: they are relayed in the language the issuing
  service publishes them in and never machine-translated, because an official
  safety document is not something to paraphrase.
- The offline cache holds the app, never the weather. wanderbar starts without a
  network and shows the last forecast that arrived, always stamped with when it
  was fetched. Age is graded on one scale: past two hours the freshness line
  turns, past six a notice states the age in words, and past twelve the verdict
  is withdrawn and the timeline greyed, because a forecast that old describes
  hours already gone. Map tiles are never cached, as bulk tile storage is
  against the OpenTopoMap and OpenStreetMap usage policies, so offline the map
  background is absent and says so.
- Positioning is 2D. GPS altitude is the wrong datum, so it is stored for
  diagnostics and read by nothing.
- Elevation is single-source per track, all-GPX or all-DEM, because mixing them
  fabricates ascent at every boundary.

## Data sources

- Forecast: Open-Meteo (blends ECMWF, GFS, ICON), fetched per waypoint.
- Cross-check: Norwegian Meteorological Institute / Yr. When the two disagree on
  temperature or rain, the timeline says so instead of quietly picking one.
- Elevation: the GPX file, else Open-Meteo's Copernicus DEM.
- Map tiles: OpenTopoMap from OpenStreetMap data. Weather icons: MET Norway.
- Avalanche bulletins: SLF (Switzerland), avalanche.report (Tyrol, South Tyrol,
  Trentino), Varsom/NVE (Norway), Avalanche Canada. Shown unaltered and always
  linked back to the issuing service.
